title: CSS: Making the Game Beautiful
subtitle: Let's Bring Our Design to Life

scenes.name: Lesson opener
scenes.visual: Lesson card: 'LESSON 3 · CSS' green tile, 'Making the Game Beautiful'.
scenes.onScreen: LESSON 3 · CSS: Making the Game Beautiful

scenes.name: Recap and promise
scenes.visual: Lesson 2's plain preview. On 'into this' a vertical wipe reveals the finished, styled game with cards. The two sit side by side, labelled BEFORE and AFTER.

lines.text: Welcome back, creators! Last time, we built the structure of Number Match with HTML.
Today, we start turning this plain page... into this!
This is the power of CSS.

scenes.name: Create style.css and link it
scenes.visual: IDE. The cursor clicks new file and types style.css; the file appears under index.html with the CSS icon. Then index.html is opened, the cursor goes to the line before </head>, and <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> types in. Labels sit on rel and href, and a connector arrow runs from href to style.css in the sidebar.

lines.text: CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It controls how our webpage looks: the colours, the sizes, the spacing, and even the movement.
Click the new file button, type style dot C S S, and press Enter.
lines.caption: Click the new file button, type style.css, and press Enter.

lines.text: We keep our styles in their own file. That way, HTML looks after the structure, CSS looks after the style, and everything stays tidy.
Now go back to index dot html. Inside the head, just before the closing head tag, type this link.
lines.caption: Now go back to index.html. Inside the <head>, just before the closing </head> tag, type this link.

lines.text: Rel equals stylesheet tells the browser that this is a style file. And H ref tells it where to find it: style dot C S S.
lines.caption: rel="stylesheet" tells the browser that this is a style file. And href tells it where to find it: style.css.

scenes.name: Selectors, properties and values
scenes.visual: A large teaching panel with the body rule at 44px. Parts light up in sync: selector (red bracket 'WHICH element'), curly brackets ('declaration block'), property ('WHAT to change'), colon, value ('HOW'), semicolon ('end of sentence'). A preview strip beside it turns pale green.
scenes.transition: Zoom into 'Quicksand' and cut to the browser.

lines.text: Let's write our first CSS rule.
First comes the selector. It tells the browser which elements we want to style. Here, we choose the body.
Then a pair of curly brackets. Everything inside them is called a declaration block.
Inside, we write a property, a colon, and a value. Background color is the property, and this colour code is the value.
lines.caption: Inside, we write a property, a colon, and a value. background-color is the property, and this colour code is the value.

lines.text: And every declaration ends with a semicolon, like a full stop at the end of a sentence.
The second declaration sets our font family to Quicksand. But wait! The browser needs to download Quicksand first.
lines.caption: The second declaration sets our font-family to Quicksand. But wait! The browser needs to download Quicksand first.

scenes.name: Google Fonts and Quicksand
scenes.visual: A generic browser frame with the address fonts.google.com, showing a simplified, non-branded mock of the steps: search 'Quicksand', the font page, 'Get font', 'Get embed code', weight chips 400–700, the <link> code box and its copy button. Then back in the IDE, the three lines paste into <head> above the style.css link. RECOMMENDED: replace the mock with a real screen recording of Google Fonts (see risks).
scenes.camera: Follow the cursor, zooming on each button pressed.
scenes.transition: Code scrolls to the top of style.css.

lines.text: Websites can use thousands of different fonts. Many of them are free on Google Fonts.
Open your browser and go to fonts dot google dot com.
lines.caption: Open your browser and go to fonts.google.com.

lines.text: Search for Quicksand, and click on it.
Click Get font, and then Get embed code.
Make sure the weights we need are chosen, from four hundred up to seven hundred. The higher the number, the bolder the text.
lines.caption: Make sure the weights we need are chosen, from 400 up to 700. The higher the number, the bolder the text.

lines.text: Now copy the link code that Google gives us.
Back in Paisley Studio, paste it inside the head, above our style sheet link.
lines.caption: Back in Paisley Studio, paste it inside the <head>, above our stylesheet link.

lines.text: The two preconnect lines help the font load quickly, and the last link downloads Quicksand itself.
Remember: the browser needs an internet connection to download a Google Font.

scenes.name: CSS variables
scenes.visual: style.css: the :root block types in. Each variable gets a colour swatch chip. Demo: --red changes from red to purple and the brand mark, heading span, progress fill and card borders all change at once in the preview; then it changes back.
scenes.sfx: Typing, a 'whoop' on the colour swap.

lines.text: Now let's build our design, starting with our colours.
At the very top of style dot C S S, we create CSS variables, inside root.
lines.caption: At the very top of style.css, we create CSS variables, inside :root.

lines.text: A variable is a colour with a name. Dash dash green is our deep forest green. Dash dash red is our bright red.
lines.caption: A variable is a colour with a name. --green is our deep forest green. --red is our bright red.

lines.text: To use a variable, we write var, and then the name in brackets.
lines.caption: To use a variable, we write var(), with the name inside the brackets.

lines.text: Here's why that's so clever. If we change dash dash red in one place...
lines.caption: Here's why that's so clever. If we change --red in one place...

lines.text: ...every part of the design that uses it changes too!

scenes.name: Page, header, panel, stats, progress
scenes.visual: One CSS rule at a time types in, about 26px, with the matching part of the live preview outlined as it changes: app-shell centres, the topbar becomes a row, the heading turns big and green, the panel becomes a white rounded box, the stats become three columns, and the progress track appears. Flex and grid diagrams show as simple flat arrows.
scenes.camera: Code left, preview right. The preview zooms to each region.
scenes.onScreen: display: flex · justify-content: space-between · display: grid · repeat(3, 1fr)
scenes.transition: Zoom into an empty card slot.

lines.text: Next, the page and the header.
The app shell keeps our game a comfortable width, and margin zero auto places it in the middle.
lines.caption: The .app-shell keeps our game a comfortable width, and margin: 0 auto places it in the middle.

lines.text: The top bar uses display flex, which lines things up in a row. Justify content space between pushes the brand to the left, and the tag to the right.
lines.caption: The .topbar uses display: flex, which lines things up in a row. justify-content: space-between pushes the brand to the left, and the tag to the right.

lines.text: The heading becomes big, bold and green, and the span inside it turns red.
The game panel gets a white background, a border, and rounded corners.
The stats use display grid, with three equal columns, one for each box.
lines.caption: The stats use display: grid, with three equal columns, one for each box.

lines.text: And the progress fill is red. Its width starts at zero percent. Later, JavaScript will make it grow.

scenes.name: Designing the number card
scenes.visual: SIGNATURE SCENE. Deep-green stage, one big card at centre (about 520px tall), with the CSS for each step shown beside it. Steps: white rectangle → corners round → 5px red border draws on → red circle grows from a square (border-radius animates 0 → 50%) → white numeral 1 drops in at centre → 'One' types underneath. Then the original reference card slides in beside it (fruit-free comparison; the reference image's apple is covered by a 'not used' tag). Finally a 4-column grid of cards fills in.
scenes.camera: Slow orbit (rotateY ±8°) around the card while it builds.
scenes.onScreen: border-radius · border: 5px solid var(--red) · border-radius: 50% · display: grid; place-items: center · font-size · font-weight: 700
scenes.sfx: Soft whoosh per step, chime on completion.
scenes.transition: The card spins (flip) into the next scene.

lines.text: Now for my favourite part: the number card. Our grid is still empty, because JavaScript will create the cards in a later lesson. So let's zoom in and design one card right now.
We start with a white rectangle.
Border radius rounds the corners.
lines.caption: border-radius rounds the corners.

lines.text: Then a thick red border, five pixels wide.
Inside, the number circle. Its width and height are equal, and border radius fifty percent turns a square into a perfect circle.
lines.caption: Inside, the number circle. Its width and height are equal, and border-radius: 50% turns a square into a perfect circle.

lines.text: Background color makes it red.
lines.caption: background-color makes it red.

lines.text: Display grid and place items center put the number exactly in the middle.
lines.caption: display: grid and place-items: center put the number exactly in the middle.

lines.text: Font size makes the number large, and font weight seven hundred makes it bold.
lines.caption: font-size makes the number large, and font-weight: 700 makes it bold.

lines.text: And finally, the number word underneath.
Here's our card next to the original design. The same bold style, made with code!
The game grid places our cards in four columns, with a gap between them.

scenes.name: Transforms and transitions
scenes.visual: A card at centre with its two faces pulled apart in 3D (exploded view): the green back with '?' and 'FLIP ME', and the white front. rotateY(180deg) is shown with a curved arrow and a protractor. The faces snap back together. A slider labelled .is-flipped switches on and the card flips with the real .55s cubic-bezier. A side-by-side comparison shows a flip with and without a transition. Then .is-matched turns the card green.
scenes.onScreen: transform: rotateY(180deg) · backface-visibility: hidden · transition: transform .55s · .is-flipped · .is-matched
scenes.sfx: Flip sound in sync, match chime.
scenes.transition: The card shrinks into a phone outline.

lines.text: But how do the cards flip over?
Every card has two faces: a green back, and a white front.
Transform rotate Y, one hundred and eighty degrees, spins an element around, like turning a page.
lines.caption: transform: rotateY(180deg) spins an element around, like turning a page.

lines.text: The front starts already turned around, and backface visibility hidden makes the side facing away invisible.
lines.caption: The front starts already turned around, and backface-visibility: hidden makes the side facing away invisible.

lines.text: When a card gets the class is flipped, the inside turns around, and the number appears.
lines.caption: When a card gets the class is-flipped, the inside turns around, and the number appears.

lines.text: The transition makes the turn smooth instead of sudden. It takes just over half a second.
And when a pair matches, the class is matched turns the border and the circle green.
lines.caption: And when a pair matches, the class is-matched turns the border and the circle green.

scenes.name: Responsive design
scenes.visual: Desktop browser and phone outline side by side showing the same styled page. The @media (max-width: 650px) block types in, and its rules highlight one at a time while the phone version updates: thinner borders, smaller gap, smaller numerals.
scenes.camera: Pans between the desktop and phone.
scenes.transition: Pull back to the whole design.

lines.text: Last one. People will play our game on computers, tablets and phones.
A media query lets us change styles when the screen is small. Max width six hundred and fifty pixels means: only on screens six hundred and fifty pixels wide or narrower.
lines.caption: A media query lets us change styles when the screen is small. max-width: 650px means: only on screens 650 pixels wide or narrower.

lines.text: On small screens, the cards get thinner borders, smaller gaps, and smaller numbers, so everything still fits.
That's called responsive design.

scenes.name: Closing
scenes.visual: Run is clicked: the styled page (empty grid) in the preview. Then the single designed card sits centre frame, still. On 'They need a brain' a gold outline of a brain/lightbulb icon pulses above it. End card: 'Next: JavaScript: Giving Our Game a Brain'.
scenes.onScreen: Next: JavaScript: Giving Our Game a Brain

lines.text: Look at what we have created!
Our simple page is now becoming a beautiful game.
But our cards still need something important.
They need a brain.
Next, we are going to introduce JavaScript, and teach our game how to think!
